newsitem.title: USA: Ruiz Massieu says had nothing to do with drugs.
newsitem.headline: Ruiz Massieu says had nothing to do with drugs.

text.p: A former Mexican deputy attorney general testified on Thursday that money the U.S. government says he got illegally for protecting drug-traffickers came in part from lavish bonuses paid to government officials.

Mario Ruiz Massieu, fighting to keep a $9 million Texas bank account from confiscation by the United States, told an eight-person jury that while his official salary in the attorney general's office was $1,000 a month, he actually received monthly bonuses of $100,000 and more from a secret budget controlled by the president of Mexico.
All this, he testified, was a product of Mexico's political system in which the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and its leaders functioned with absolute impugnity.
"Mexico is a country without rules," Ruiz Massieu said.
"The PRI is like a state party, like the Communist Party in the (former) Soviet Union ... the state party and the government are the same thing," he said. "They have formed the perfect dictatorship."

Earlier witnesses in the four-day-old civil trial said that Ruiz Massieu received money from drug-traffickers in exchange for protection while he was a deputy attorney general for two separate periods in 1993 and 1994. The U.S. government is trying to confiscate his account in Texas Commerce Bank on grounds that it was all drug money.
He also said he never had responsibility for fighting drugs.

Ruiz Massieu, in testimony that was to continue on Friday, implied that it would have been impossible for him to provide protection for drug-traffickers. He said that while in the attorney general's office, he was in charge not of combatting drugs, but other crimes.
"I was never responsible for the fight against drugs," Ruiz Massieu said.

His testimony also included a lengthy explanation of the government's bonus system, in which he said those in management positions received "100 times more" than their official salaries. His brother, Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, got bonuses totalling between $25 million and $30 million starting in 1987 during his time as governor of the state of Guerrero and later general secretary of the PRI, he said.

Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu was assassinated in Mexico City in September 1994. Attorneys for Mario Ruiz Massieu said in opening arguments on Monday that the attempt to seize his money was part of a campaign of vengeance by the Mexican government, conducted with the aid of the United States, because he charged that the PRI obstructed an investigation into Jose Francisco's death.

Ruiz Massieu has said in pre-trial depositions that the hefty bonuses he and his brother received went, at least in part, into the Texas bank acount, which he opened in 1993. The rest came from his father and brother as the family pooled its money to place in the United States to protect against instability in Mexico.

His father, Armando Ruiz Quintanilla, also in Thursday testimony, upheld his son's version of events, saying he personally put $2 million into the family pool and gave his sons "total" control over the money, all without a written contract.

Before Ruiz Massieu took the stand, U.S. District Judge Nancy Atlas, acting on a defence motion that the government had not proved its case, found that there was probable cause to believe the government was right.
Her ruling meant that the jury will make the final decision in deliberations that were expected to begin on Friday after Ruiz Massieu completed his testimony and closing arguments.
